charts.title: Correlation of inertia and recovery across people, under the planned inertia measure and the usual all-pairs one.
charts.takeaway: r was negative in all 4 datasets, from −0.28 to −0.44: people whose mood carries over more recover less of a swing. With all-pairs inertia the size rose to 0.67 to 0.81.
charts.units: Pearson correlation r across people, −1 to 1; further below 0 means more carryover goes with less recovery. Inertia is how much of one prompt's mood carries into the next. Recovery is the share of a large swing that is gone by the next prompt. r is the correlation of the two across people
charts.n: 0018: 71 of 999 people eligible; 0062: 49 of 321 people eligible; 0008: 99 of 114 people eligible; 0076: 259 of 519 people eligible
charts.baseline: All-pairs inertia, the usual definition. It reuses the same prompt pairs that recovery is computed from, so part of its correlation is built in
series_names: Planned measure: inertia from pairs that are not spikes

axis.label: r across people (below 0: more carryover, less recovery)

charts.title: Size of the inertia and recovery correlation in each dataset, against people simulated with one parameter.
charts.takeaway: The coupling was weaker than the one-parameter null in 2 of 4 datasets: 0008 at 0.279 against a 5th percentile of 0.367, and 0018 at 0.4391 against 0.4399. The other 2 sat inside the null.
charts.units: size of r, from 0 to 1; lower means inertia and recovery vary more separately across people. Inertia is how much of one prompt's mood carries into the next. Recovery is the share of a large swing that is gone by the next prompt. r is the correlation of the two across people
charts.n: 0018: 71 of 999 people eligible; 0062: 49 of 321 people eligible; 0008: 99 of 114 people eligible; 0076: 259 of 519 people eligible; 200, 156, 200, 200 usable null draws
charts.interval: 5th to 95th percentile of the null draws
charts.baseline: One-parameter AR(1) null: simulated people whose mood follows a single carryover number, placed on the real prompt schedules. In that world inertia and recovery are one trait
charts.threshold: Size of r below the null's 5th percentile, with the 95% interval of r inside −0.7 to 0.7
charts.ruled_out: In 0062 and 0076 a one-parameter account is not ruled out: the sizes 0.414 and 0.289 sit above the null 5th percentiles 0.215 and 0.168
charts.value_name: size of r in the real data

axis.label: size of r (lower: the two measures vary more separately)

charts.title: The three rules set in advance, checked in each dataset.
charts.takeaway: The shuffle check held in 4 of 4 datasets and the separate-variation rule in 2 of 4. Two factors beat one in 0 of 3 fitted datasets, with p from 0.81 to 1.00.
charts.units: mean inertia for the shuffle rule; size of r for the null rule; p of the chi-square difference test (a test of whether the larger model fits better) for the factor rule

charts.title: Split-half reliability of each person's inertia and recovery.
charts.takeaway: Reliability ran from 0.03 to 0.47, far from 1, so a person's odd-day and even-day scores barely agree and the two-factor test had little power.
charts.units: split-half reliability: the correlation across people between a measure computed on odd days and the same measure on even days. 1 is a perfectly repeatable measure, 0 is noise
charts.n: 0018: 53 people; 0008: 60 people; 0076: 152 people. Dataset 0062 could not be fitted (5 persons with both halves, fewer than 30)
charts.no_interval: The result file gives one split-half correlation for each measure and dataset, with no interval.
charts.baseline: A reliability of 1, a measure that gives the same person the same score on both halves
